elements.name: Exceptional Value
elements.what: A distinguished value object representing circumstances outside normal ranges (missing, invalid, not-applicable) that flows through domain computations in place of a normal Whole Value.
elements.problem: Domain models must keep computing in the presence of missing or exceptional inputs without littering every method with special-case checks or aborting user workflows.
elements.named_in: Cunningham, 'The CHECKS Pattern Language of Information Integrity' (PLoP 1994; c2.com/ppr/checks.html, loaded live)
tags: borderline: overlaps Special Case (Fowler) and Null Object, but the CHECKS mechanism is a value that propagates through arithmetic/computation rather than a polymorphic do-nothing object
elements.borderline: Close to special-case / null-object already in index; kept because the propagating-value mechanism is distinct and the charter names it explicitly.

elements.name: Meaningless Behavior
elements.what: Write domain methods without defensive input checks; let computations on exceptional/missing values fail or yield meaningless results, and have the input/output boundary recover (e.g. display blank) instead.
elements.problem: Defensive checks duplicated through every domain method obscure the model; centering recovery at the presentation boundary keeps domain code minimal while tolerating bad data.
elements.named_in: Cunningham, 'The CHECKS Pattern Language of Information Integrity' (PLoP 1994; c2.com/ppr/checks.html, loaded live)

elements.name: Deferred Validation
elements.what: Delay comprehensive validity checking of captured data until an action requires it, scaling the rigor of the check to the consequences of that action (edit freely, validate on save/commit/publish).
elements.problem: Eager validation at entry time rejects legitimately incomplete in-progress data and hard-codes one rigidity level; different actions need different degrees of integrity.
elements.named_in: Cunningham, 'The CHECKS Pattern Language of Information Integrity' (PLoP 1994; c2.com/ppr/checks.html, loaded live)

elements.name: Composed Method
aka: compose methods out of intention-revealing calls
elements.what: Divide a program into methods that each perform one identifiable task at a single level of abstraction, composed of calls whose names state intent.
elements.problem: Methods mixing abstraction levels are hard to read, reuse, and override; keeping each method small and single-level makes control flow self-documenting and refactorable.
elements.named_in: Beck, Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns (1997)
elements.borderline: Sits near the practices boundary, but it is a named, recurring structural construct (the canonical target shape of Extract Method), not a process item. Distinct from Combined Method (Henney) already in index.

elements.name: Method Object
aka: Replace Method with Method Object (Fowler, Refactoring)
Replace Function with Command (Fowler, Refactoring 2nd ed.)
elements.what: Reify a complex method as its own class whose fields hold the method's parameters and temporaries, turning locals into instance state so the computation can be decomposed into helper methods.
elements.problem: A long method whose many local variables defeat extraction cannot be decomposed in place; hoisting the computation into an object removes the local-variable coupling.
elements.named_in: Beck, Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns (1997); named as a refactoring target in Fowler, Refactoring
tags: distinct from function-object (functor) already in index

elements.name: Pluggable Selector
elements.what: Store the name (selector) of a method in an instance variable and dispatch on it reflectively, so instances of one class exhibit different behavior without subclassing.
elements.problem: A family of trivially differing subclasses (each overriding one small method) is overkill; parameterizing instances by a stored selector collapses the hierarchy.
elements.named_in: Beck, Smalltalk Best Practice Patterns (1997)
tags: also used in xUnit test-method dispatch

elements.name: Product Trader
elements.what: Clients create objects by naming an abstract product class plus a specification; a trader maps specifications to concrete product classes and performs the instantiation.
elements.problem: Direct constructor calls couple clients to concrete classes; a trader decouples client from product, easing configuration and evolution of class hierarchies and frameworks.
elements.named_in: Baeumer & Riehle, 'Product Trader', PLoPD3 (1997) (riehle.org paper page and PLoPD3 ToC loaded live)

elements.name: Sponsor-Selector
elements.what: Separate three responsibilities — sponsors that know when a resource is useful, a selector that picks among sponsors' recommendations, and the client that uses the chosen resource — to select the best resource dynamically.
elements.problem: A system must choose the best of a dynamically changing set of resources/strategies without hard-coding selection knowledge into the client.
elements.named_in: Wallingford, 'Sponsor-Selector: A Pattern Language for Choosing the Best Resource', PLoPD3 (1997) (cs.uni.edu/~wallingf/patterns/sponsor-selector.html verified)

elements.name: Bureaucracy
elements.what: A compound pattern composing Composite, Mediator, Chain of Responsibility, and Observer to build self-maintaining hierarchical structures where each level mediates its children and escalates requests upward.
elements.problem: Hierarchies (documents, GUIs, organizations) must maintain internal consistency and route interactions across levels without external coordination logic.
elements.named_in: Riehle, 'Bureaucracy', PLoPD3 (1997) (PLoPD3 ToC loaded live)
elements.borderline: Compound of four patterns already in the index; kept as an independently named, published composite mechanism.

elements.name: Diagnostic Logger
elements.what: Route all diagnostic messages through a dedicated logger object that decouples message producers from output destinations, formats, and severity filtering.
elements.problem: Ad-hoc prints scatter diagnostic policy through the code; a central logger lets destination, format, and level be configured without touching call sites.
elements.named_in: Harrison, 'Patterns for Logging Diagnostic Messages', PLoPD3 (1997) (PLoPD3 ToC loaded live); living realizations: log4j/syslog-style logging frameworks

elements.name: Diagnostic Context
elements.what: Attach per-thread/per-request key-value context (transaction id, user, request id) to a stash that the logging system automatically appends to every message emitted within that scope.
elements.problem: Interleaved logs from concurrent activities are unattributable; carrying context explicitly through every call is invasive, so the logger holds it ambiently per execution scope.
elements.named_in: Harrison, 'Patterns for Logging Diagnostic Messages', PLoPD3 (1997); canonical living form: log4j/logback/SLF4J MDC/NDC documentation

elements.name: Abstract Session
elements.what: A server object hands each client an opaque session object encapsulating the per-client state of their conversation; the client makes further requests through the session rather than the server, with full type safety.
elements.problem: A service serving many clients must keep per-client state without exposing its internals or forcing clients to pass identity/state tokens on every call (the untyped-handle alternative).
elements.named_in: Pryce, 'Abstract Session: An Object Structural Pattern', PLoPD4 (2000) (PLoPD4 ToC loaded live; c2 AbstractSessionPattern page exists)

elements.name: Object Recursion
elements.what: Distribute the handling of a request recursively over a polymorphic object structure: each recurser handles its part and delegates the remainder to its successor(s) until terminator objects stop the recursion.
elements.problem: A request must be processed piecewise along a linked/hierarchical structure; centralizing the traversal in one loop couples it to the structure, while polymorphic recursion keeps each node's contribution local.
elements.named_in: Woolf, 'The Object Recursion Pattern', PLoPD4 (2000) (PLoPD4 ToC loaded live)
elements.borderline: Generalizes the traversal shared by Composite, Decorator, Chain of Responsibility and Interpreter (all in index); kept because it is independently named and distinguishes handle-vs-forward semantics.

elements.name: Relationship Object
elements.what: Reify a relationship between objects as a first-class object that stores the participants plus the relationship's own attributes and behavior, instead of encoding the link as mutual references.
elements.problem: Relationships with their own state (start date, role, quantity) or lifecycle cannot live naturally inside either participant; direct mutual pointers scatter the relationship's logic and complicate consistency.
elements.named_in: Noble, 'Basic Relationship Patterns', PLoPD4 (2000); also Boyd, 'Business Patterns of Association Objects', PLoPD3 (1997) (both ToCs loaded live)

elements.name: Temporal Property
elements.what: Represent an attribute (or whole object) as a time-indexed collection of values so the model can answer 'what was/is/will be the value at time T' rather than only the current value.
elements.problem: Domain data changes over time and past states must remain queryable (retroactive corrections, effective dates); overwriting in place destroys history.
elements.named_in: Carlson, Estepp & Fowler, 'Temporal Patterns', PLoPD4 (2000) (ToC loaded live); living treatment: Fowler's eaaDev temporal patterns (Temporal Property, Temporal Object, Snapshot, Effectivity)

elements.name: Audit Log
elements.what: Record every significant change or event as an appended, timestamped entry alongside the current state, so history can be inspected without reconstructing it from the model.
elements.problem: Systems need an inspectable record of what changed, when, and by whom, without adopting full temporal modeling or event sourcing as the source of truth.
elements.named_in: Fowler, 'Temporal Patterns' (with Carlson & Estepp), PLoPD4 (2000); living treatment: Fowler eaaDev 'Audit Log'
tags: distinct from event-sourcing (log is secondary record, not source of truth)

elements.name: Comparand
elements.what: Equip objects with a dedicated comparand value used solely for cheap identity/equality testing, avoiding expensive structural comparison or unreliable address comparison.
elements.problem: Identity tests on structured objects are frequent and must be fast; comparing full contents is costly and comparing addresses breaks when objects are copied or serialized.
elements.named_in: 'The Comparand Pattern: Cheap Identity Testing Using Dedicated Values', PLoPD5 ch. 8 (2006) (Library of Congress ToC loaded live)
tags: related to interning (sharing, in index) but distinct mechanism
elements.borderline: Obscure; named at chapter-title level in a published volume, mechanism stated in the title. Merge team may fold into sharing/interning if judged too thin.

elements.name: Generation Gap
elements.what: Keep machine-generated code in a core base class that is never edited, and put all hand-written modifications in a subclass that survives regeneration unchanged.
elements.problem: Generated code is overwritten on every regeneration, destroying manual edits; separating generated and hand-written code by inheritance makes modifications durable across regenerations.
elements.named_in: Vlissides, 'Generation Gap', Pattern Hatching: Design Patterns Applied (1998; earlier C++ Report 1996)
tags: still standard in GUI builders / ORM / protocol-compiler output

elements.name: Fast Path
elements.what: Provide a short, cheap code path for the common case (often lock-free or per-CPU) and fall back to a general, heavier slow path for the rare or complex cases.
elements.problem: Optimizing an entire algorithm for the worst case penalizes the dominant case; splitting paths buys common-case speed while keeping rare-case correctness in simpler code.
elements.named_in: McKenney, 'Selecting Locking Designs for Parallel Programs', PLoPD2 (1996) — Parallel Fastpath (verified via rdrop.com paper/perfbook); Meszaros, capacity pattern language, PLoPD1 (1995)

elements.name: Credit-Based Flow Control
elements.what: A receiver grants the sender explicit credits, each authorizing transmission of one unit; the sender stops when credits run out and resumes as the receiver replenishes them from freed buffer space.
elements.problem: A producer must never overrun a consumer's buffering capacity; explicit credits achieve lossless flow control without dropping or blind rate guessing.
elements.named_in: Kung & Morris, 'Credit-Based Flow Control for ATM Networks', IEEE Network (1995); Meszaros, capacity pattern language, PLoPD1 (1995); Reactive Streams specification (request(n) demand)
elements.borderline: Specific mechanism beneath the general backpressure element (in index) and sibling of sliding-window-flow-control (in index); kept because the credit mechanism is independently named and distinct from windowed ack-based control.

parked_architecture.name: Recursive Control (Selic, PLoPD3)
parked_architecture.why: Structuring pattern for whole real-time control systems (hierarchy of control components); system-level structure, fails altitude upward.

parked_architecture.name: Bodyguard (das Neves & Garrido, PLoPD3)
parked_architecture.why: Sharing and protecting objects across address spaces in distributed systems without full RPC; distribution-level.

parked_architecture.name: Object Synchronizer (Silva, Pereira & Marques, PLoPD4)
parked_architecture.why: Synchronization policy for distributed object replicas; distribution-level.

parked_architecture.name: Single Access Point + Check Point (Yoder & Barcalow, PLoPD4)
parked_architecture.why: Presented as 'Architectural Patterns for Enabling Application Security'; application-entry security structure, Phase 3 territory.

parked_architecture.name: Dynamic Object Model / Adaptive Object Model (Riehle, Tilman & Johnson, PLoPD5)
parked_architecture.why: Yoder/Johnson describe it as an architectural style; its design-level constituents (Type Object, Property/attribute objects, Strategy, Interpreter) are already in the catalog.

excluded_notable.name: Whole Value (CHECKS)
excluded_notable.why: Already folded into the index: newtype carries 'whole value (related CHECKS pattern)' as aka, and quantity covers the unit-bearing case. No separate entry proposed; merge team may promote if it prefers CHECKS naming.

excluded_notable.name: Echo Back (CHECKS)
excluded_notable.why: UI interaction feedback (redisplay interpreted input for user verification); interaction-design guidance rather than an implementable software mechanism — fails the altitude test sideways.

excluded_notable.name: Visible Implication (CHECKS)
excluded_notable.why: Display of derived quantities for user review; the mechanism half (computed/derived values) is covered by reactive-signals' computed/derivations aka; the rest is UI guidance.

excluded_notable.name: Instant Projection / Hypothetical Publication / Forecast Confirmation / Diagnostic Query (CHECKS)
excluded_notable.why: Publication-workflow and inspection-process patterns, above/os-outside the single-program mechanism band.

excluded_notable.name: Cascade (Beck SBPP)
excluded_notable.why: Smalltalk message-cascade syntax (';'); raw language syntax. The general mechanism is covered by fluent-interface (in index).

excluded_notable.name: Pluggable Object (Beck SBPP)
excluded_notable.why: Parameterize behavior by plugging in an object instead of subclassing — folds into Strategy (in index); Pluggable Selector kept as the genuinely distinct reflective variant.

excluded_notable.name: Abstract Class (Woolf, PLoPD4)
excluded_notable.why: Design principle / language-feature usage guidance, not a nameable mechanism.

excluded_notable.name: Essence (Carlson, PLoPD4)
excluded_notable.why: Staged construction with completeness validation before yielding the real object — folds into Builder + Smart Constructor (both in index).

excluded_notable.name: Object Recovery (Silva et al., PLoPD3)
excluded_notable.why: Object-level state save/restore — folds into Memento + Checkpointing + Rollback (all in index).

excluded_notable.name: Manager (Sommerlad, PLoPD3) and Domain Object Manager (PLoPD5)
excluded_notable.why: Same mechanism as object-manager already in index (lifecycle + lookup of a class's instances); recommend adding 'Manager (Sommerlad)' and 'Domain Object Manager' as aka on object-manager.

excluded_notable.name: Encapsulated Context (Kelly, PLoPD5)
excluded_notable.why: Same mechanism as context-object (in index); recommend aka merge.

excluded_notable.name: Default Visitor / Extrinsic Visitor (Nordberg, PLoPD3)
excluded_notable.why: Visitor variants; fold as aka under visitor (in index).

excluded_notable.name: Code Locking / Data Locking / Data Ownership (McKenney, PLoPD2)
excluded_notable.why: Already covered: coarse-grained-lock, lock-striping, and thread-specific-storage (which carries 'data ownership' as aka).

excluded_notable.name: Match Progress Work with New Work / Finish Work in Progress / Share the Load / Work Shed at Periphery (Meszaros, PLoPD1)
excluded_notable.why: Capacity-tuning policy guidance; established siblings already in index (load-shedding, fresh-work-before-stale, leaky-bucket-counter). Work Shed at Periphery folds into load-shedding aka.

notes: Gap hunt over CHECKS (primary page c2.com/ppr/checks.html loaded live, all ten patterns altitude-tested), Beck SBPP, and PLoPD1-5 (PLoPD3 ToC via riehle.org, PLoPD4 ToC via InformIT, PLoPD5 ToC via LoC catdir - all loaded live this session). Confirmed already in index before proposing anything: Null Object, Twin, Role Object, Type Object, Command Processor, Serializer, Half-Object plus Protocol (charter said 'park' but it is already IN the index as a communication element - no action), Collecting Parameter, Execute Around Method, Double Dispatch, Delegation, Acceptor-Connector, Asynchronous Completion Token, Double-Checked Locking, External Polymorphism, Acyclic Visitor, Extension Object, Proactor, Guard Clause, Riding Over Transients, Leaky Bucket Counter, Fresh Work Before Stale, Load Shedding. INDEX ISSUES SPOTTED: (1) lines 457-458 'setjmp-longjmp-exception-handling' and 'setjmp-longjmp-structured-error-handling' look like an unmerged duplicate pair; (2) GoF Decorator exists ONLY as an aka on adapter ('aka: Wrapper, Decorator') - wrong fold, Decorator is a distinct GoF pattern and should be its own element; (3) GoF Prototype exists ONLY as an aka on factory-method ('aka: Virtual Constructor, Prototype, clone') - also a wrong fold, Prototype should be its own element. I did not add Decorator/Prototype myself (outside charter; fix is an index correction, not a new proposal). Naming caution for merge: composed-method (Beck) is distinct from combined-method (Henney, in index) despite similar names; method-object is distinct from function-object (functor). 'Late Creation' as an aka for Product Trader could not be verified and was dropped. Comparand is the only needs-scrutiny entry (chapter-title-level naming only). Yield: 20 elements, mostly the CHECKS/Beck/PLoPD3-5 set the charter predicted plus a genuine logging gap (no logger element existed in the 577) and two systems mechanisms (fast path, credit-based flow control) surfaced by the PLoPD1/2 sweep.
